name: Tetrahydrozoline drops (Visine)

lead: Visine-type drops contain tetrahydrozoline, a vasoconstrictor that shrinks surface blood vessels in the eye to reduce redness. Looksmaxxers use them for whiter sclera.

The redness-relief effect is established and the product is sold over the counter for short-term use. Reference sources describe rebound redness after prolonged use, and no study has examined it as a cosmetic treatment.

paras: Tetrahydrozoline is an alpha-adrenergic agonist acting on alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors, constricting vessels on the eye surface. Effects start within minutes and its half-life is about 6 hours.

Prolonged use can lead to tolerance and rebound redness, and eye drops may cause blurred vision, irritation and dilated pupils. Swallowing the product can cause serious poisoning, especially in children, with no antidote. Labels advise seeing a doctor for persistent redness and removing contact lenses first.

forums.title: Cycling Lumify and Visine to not build a tolerance

lead: Tetrahydrozoline (also spelled tetryzoline) is an over-the-counter vasoconstrictor used in eye drops and nasal sprays. The best-known redness-relief eye drop containing it is Visine, which contains 0.05 percent tetrahydrozoline hydrochloride and is sold to temporarily relieve eye redness from minor irritations [1][2].

In looksmaxxing communities such drops are discussed as a quick way to whiten the sclera and brighten the eyes. Reference sources note that tetrahydrozoline is not meant for prolonged use because tolerance can develop and stopping it can cause rebound redness [1], and forum users themselves frequently mention rebound as a drawback and compare it unfavorably with brimonidine-based drops [3]. Accidental or deliberate oral ingestion can cause serious poisoning, particularly in children [1].
infobox: Visine (introduced late 1950s; now marketed by Kenvue)
OTC (US monograph for short-term redness relief)

paras: Tetrahydrozoline is used to relieve redness of the eye from minor irritants, and can be combined with antazoline for allergic conjunctivitis [1]. Visine redness products carry 0.05 percent tetrahydrozoline hydrochloride and, per Grokipedia, fall under the US FDA over-the-counter monograph for ophthalmic drugs as safe and effective for short-term relief of redness from minor irritation. Other Visine lines contain lubricants such as polyethylene glycol or hypromellose, or antihistamines for allergy symptoms [2].
In looksmaxxing forums, users describe using redness drops to make the whites of the eyes look clearer, usually as a short-term measure [3].

Tetrahydrozoline is an alpha-adrenergic agonist acting on alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors, which constricts blood vessels in the eye; its biological half-life in healthy people is about 6 hours, with part excreted unchanged in urine [1]. Grokipedia describes the effect as beginning within minutes and localized to conjunctival vessels at normal use [2].

Wikipedia states that the drug is not intended for prolonged use because its effect wears off; after tolerance develops, stopping it can cause rebound vasodilation and more redness, and prolonged nasal use can cause rebound congestion [1]. Eye drops may cause blurred vision, irritation and pupil dilation [1]. Product labeling, as described by Grokipedia, advises consulting a doctor for persistent symptoms and cautions that overuse can cause rebound redness, eye pain or vision changes, and recommends removing contact lenses before use [2].

Oral ingestion of tetrahydrozoline can cause slowed heart rate, respiratory depression, low blood pressure, drowsiness and vomiting, and children are the most common overdose victims. There is no antidote and treatment is supportive; fatalities are rare with treatment [1]. Wikipedia also reports the substance has been involved in criminal cases of drugging, and notes that a popular belief about it causing violent diarrhea does not reflect the actual range of effects [1]. A published case report examined drug-facilitated sexual assault involving a tetrahydrozoline eye drop [4].

Tetrahydrozoline was patented in 1954 and entered medical use in 1959 [1]. Visine was introduced by Leeming in the late 1950s (Grokipedia gives both 1957 and 1958), came under Pfizer after the company acquired Leeming in 1961, passed to Johnson & Johnson in 2006 and to Kenvue in 2023 [2]. Some Grokipedia details are not corroborated elsewhere and its dates are inconsistent.
Older toxicology research has also examined Visine as an adulterant in urine drug-screen testing and reported effects on cannabinoid immunoassays [5][6].

On looksmax.org, a poster describes using redness drops to make eyes look lighter and proposes alternating tetrahydrozoline and brimonidine drops to avoid tolerance and mask rebound, while a reply says Visine is stronger and causes rebound redness, making it counterproductive [3]. The poster states that eye health is being set aside for the effect. These are user opinions without clinical testing.

No studies found of tetrahydrozoline as a cosmetic eyewhitening treatment. Related published work includes a randomized comparison of Systane UD drops versus Visine Intensiv for moderate dry eye [7], and a case report of a nonpigmenting fixed drug eruption linked to tetrahydrozoline sensitivity [8].
